topic: Skadoosh: Lightning-Fast Local Voice Agent Framework in Rust
keywords: pipecat vs livekit vs rust voice agent
local vs cloud voice agent cost per minute
angles: Rust's zero-GC + zero-unsafe pitch for real-time audio: Skadoosh is #![forbid(unsafe_code)] and lock-free, arguing Rust removes Python's GIL/GC jitter (the same claim pipecrab and rustvani make) for deterministic sub-second turn-taking.

Clause-level streaming + true barge-in: TTS starts on the first clause (not the full reply) and barge-in cuts old audio in ~5–10 ms — the two features that actually decide whether a local agent feels conversational.

Batteries-included but pluggable: a 5-line SDK (Agent::builder().config(...).build()?.run()) plus SttEngine/LlmBackend/TtsEngine traits — the review should test whether the abstraction really lets you swap engines.

A genuinely unusual feature set: WASM plugin sandbox (wasmtime, no FS/network, fuel-bounded) exposed to the LLM as tools, a LAN multi-agent 'mesh' (UDP discovery + forwarding calls), RAG over local .txt/.md, and proactive --watch triggers. Nothing comparable in the competitor set.

Trust/skepticism angle (important for a review): the advertised GitHub repo 404s and the project shows contradictory identities (crates.io owner TheLimeDev vs docs.rs owner Hot-Coco; HF model renamed StealthyML → Monster-Code; CI badge points at the dead repo). ~22 releases in 6 days with 389 downloads and 0 reverse deps = early-stage, single-author, un-benchmarked.

Privacy/compliance driver: EU AI Act (voiceprints = high-risk since Aug 2025), GDPR/CPRA, HIPAA — 'no cloud, no API keys, no data leaving the machine' is now an architectural requirement, not a preference.

The realistic hardware story: default LLM is a 1.5B Qwen2.5 GGUF, so this is a small-model, local-only agent — the review should be honest that a 1.5B model trails frontier models on knowledge-heavy tasks, and that GPU features (CUDA/CoreML/DirectML/ROCm) matter for a good experience.
The 404 framework: docs and source are first-class but the public repository has vanished - what a reader can and cannot verify, and how to audit a crate straight from its .crate tarball.

Architecture deep dive: the seven-stage pipeline and its tokio task topology, and why every stage is a boxed trait object (SttEngine / LlmBackend / TtsEngine) - the pluggability story Pipecat tells in Python, done in-process in Rust.

Barge-in mechanics: flush via an AtomicU64 epoch bumped by the caller and compared inside the realtime audio callback, with clip pushes re-checking the epoch - a genuinely lock-free interrupt path. The README's 5-10 ms figure is an unverified author claim; the article should label it.

CPU-only reality check: run the RTF math stage by stage (VAD <1 ms/chunk, whisper tiny.en ~273 MB, Kokoro 1.3-1.8x on four cores but below 1x on two, Qwen2.5-1.5B at 4-8 tok/s with 200-350 ms TTFT) to show where 'lightning-fast' holds and where it does not.
Rust versus Python for voice agents: no GIL, no FFI marshalling of audio buffers, realtime-safe callback discipline versus Pipecat and LiveKit's Python plus hosted-inference default.

Feature breadth as a differentiator: WASM plugin skills (wasmtime, fuel-gated), RAG over local docs with MiniLM ONNX, a LAN agent mesh with call forwarding, proactive file/process/timer watchers, a JSON memory store, a subprocess sandbox for code_exec, hold music during tool calls, and emotion-modulated TTS speed.

Deprecation forensics and supply-chain caution: HF org rename, model-card deprecation note, 404 repo, 23 versions in five days, 389 downloads, zero reverse deps - a reproducible 'should I depend on this?' checklist.
Cost comparison: $0/min local inference versus $0.30-$0.50 per call and ~$0.01-$0.05/min managed stacks, plus the electricity and hardware offset.

Positioning map: Skadoosh (local Rust, no transport) versus Pipecat (pipeline, bring your own transport) versus LiveKit Agents (WebRTC/SIP) versus HF speech-to-speech (local Python with the Realtime protocol) versus Moshi (full-duplex speech-to-speech).
summary: Skadoosh is a dual-licensed (MIT OR Apache-2.0) Rust crate implementing a complete, fully local voice-agent pipeline: cpal mic capture (16 kHz mono) -> Silero VAD -> whisper-rs STT -> streaming OpenAI-compatible LLM (Ollama by default) -> clause splitting -> ONNX Kokoro-82M TTS -> cpal playback with lock-free barge-in. It is the most complete all-local Rust voice agent on crates.io by feature count (22,255 Rust lines, 188 #[test], #![forbid(unsafe_code)]), but it is effectively unmaintained: the documented GitHub repository returns HTTP 404 (verified via raw HTTP, api.github.com and authenticated gh CLI on 2026-10-01), the author's model card says the project 'has been deprecated', and the crate has 389 all-time downloads and zero reverse dependencies. Verdict: a strong architecture reference and a workable self-hosted build, but a risky production dependency. All performance numbers printed by the project (5-10 ms barge-in) are author claims, not third-party benchmarked.

caveats: GitHub star/fork/issue counts for Skadoosh itself cannot be verified - the repository 404s and no Wayback snapshot exists.
The 5-10 ms barge-in figure is the author's claim in the README; the mechanism (lock-free epoch flush) is verifiable in source, the timing is not.

Some third-party benchmark figures (Kokoro RTF, Qwen2.5-1.5B TTFT) were measured on different hardware and with different tooling than Skadoosh uses; treat them as indicative, not as Skadoosh benchmarks.

Skadoosh exposes a StageLatency AgentEvent (stt_ms/llm_ms/tts_ms/playback_ms) for self-measurement; no published end-to-end numbers exist, so the article should tell readers to measure rather than quote vendor claims.
Type is 'review' per the issue description even though the parent pipeline may label the post otherwise; the brief keeps type=review.
risks: Upstream repository is gone (404): no issue tracker for bug reports, no CI verification, no way to confirm docs.rs source matches the README badges.
The author's own model card states the project is deprecated; the fine-tuned default model is a third-party artifact relocated to a different Hugging Face org (Monster-Code).
389 downloads and zero reverse dependencies: effectively no external deployment validation.
TTS is the weak link on two-core CPU-only machines (Kokoro below 1x real time there), which undercuts the 'lightning-fast' positioning for laptops and Raspberry-Pi-class hardware.
Whole-utterance whisper.cpp STT behind a 300 ms silence gate is architecturally older than 2026 streaming ASR (Parakeet, Nemotron, Zipformer) used by RealtimeSTT and HF speech-to-speech.
VAD/STT/TTS/LLM defaults are English-first (whisper tiny.en, Kokoro 'af' voice) even though the crate itself is language-agnostic.
README performance numbers (5-10 ms barge-in) are author claims, not third-party benchmarked.
Bundling espeak-ng (GPL) as a runtime dependency for Kokoro phonemisation needs a licence review before shipping in a closed product.

key_points: Open-source voice agent platform (Rust server + ESP32 hardware client); ~592 stars, 77 forks.
Widely covered: Show HN posts plus an Instructables 'build your own AI voice agent' guide; strongest mindshare of the Rust voice-agent projects.
Hardware-anchored (needs the ESP32 device/board), i.e. an appliance rather than an embeddable library — the opposite trade-off from Skadoosh.
Cross-platform Rust pipeline framework for fully local, interruptible voice agents (~19 stars).
Barge-in is 'interrupt-safe by construction': a data lane plus a high-priority system lane per link, with a synchronous decide step and async perform step; Interrupt frames overtake queued work.
No executor baked in (caller drives the future); core CI-compiles for wasm32; layered core<runtime<traits<adapters enforced by a workspace test.
Explicit cross-platform matrix shows macOS/iOS/Android working while Linux/Windows are 'expected to work, not yet verified' — a real gap for server/desktop users.
From-scratch Rust port of Pipecat: frame-based pipelines, processor abstractions, interruption handling — plus a 'Dhara' conversation-flow manager and 'RAVI' protocol.
Claims production deployment for a Kerala government voice agent (Malayalam/Hindi/English); Sarvam + Gnani + 60db Indic STT integrations.
Larger/opinionated stack (axum WebSocket transport, billing/usage tracking, Postgres tool). Package is 2.5 MB source; docs.rs build FAILED for 0.3.0 — heavier setup than Skadoosh's single binary.
Local-first Rust voice AI framework: Whisper/Distil-Whisper/Sherpa STT, Kokoro/Piper/Qwen3/Pocket/Chatterbox TTS, speaker diarization, 'Live Talk' barge-in (~46 stars).
Ships an HTTP + WebSocket API and a 5-tab browser UI embedded in the binary; 'No API keys. No cloud. No data leaving your machine.'
Closest feature-level competitor to Skadoosh, but heavier surface area (diarization, multi-backend TTS) versus Skadoosh's minimal mic→speaker loop.
A 'unified Voice Layer for AI Agents' with seamless integration to existing agentic frameworks (~313 stars).
Positions as a bolt-on voice layer for agents you already built, rather than a full self-contained local pipeline.
More stars than the other Rust projects but last pushed 2026-05-31 — relatively slow cadence vs. Skadoosh's rapid releases.
Frame-based pipeline you assemble yourself: VAD -> STT -> LLM -> TTS -> transport; 16,100 stars, BSD-2-Clause, pushed 2026-10-01.
Assumes no transport, so telephony/browser/WebRTC are yours to wire; largest integration library (Deepgram, AssemblyAI, Cartesia, ElevenLabs, Gemini, OpenAI).
Vendor-neutral comparison (Fora Soft, Jul 2026): the framework barely moves latency, 'your model choice sets the number'; speech-to-speech ~300 ms vs an STT+LLM+TTS cascade at 300-800 ms.
Downside vs Skadoosh: Python, hosted models by default, no built-in local-first pipeline or in-process barge-in primitive.
Welded to LiveKit's open-source WebRTC/SIP media server: rooms, dispatch, scaling, multi-party and video come free; 14,434 stars, Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-09-30.
LiveKit's own guidance: a well-built pipeline lands ~500-650 ms P95; Turn Detector v1.0 saves 200-600 ms versus naive silence thresholding.
You work inside its agent/session shape - stages cannot be added, reordered or branched the way Skadoosh's engine traits allow.
No fully-local path: STT/LLM/TTS are hosted inference providers.
Closest architectural sibling: modular VAD -> STT -> LLM -> TTS exposed over the OpenAI Realtime GA event set (WebSocket/WebRTC); 13,359 stars, Apache-2.0.
Defaults to local Parakeet TDT STT + Qwen3-TTS with an optional fully local LLM (vLLM/llama.cpp); runs in production as the conversation backend for thousands of Reachy Mini robots.
Documented hardware floor: 16 GB+ unified memory (Apple Silicon) or ~24 GB VRAM (NVIDIA) for a fully local conversation - far heavier than Skadoosh's ~1.5 GB Q4 LLM plus 76-500 MB of speech models.
Ships the Realtime transport protocol; Skadoosh ships an in-process Rust pipeline with no network transport at all.
Full-duplex spoken dialogue model (Helium 7B backbone + 1.1 kbps Mimi codec), 11,163 stars, Apache-2.0.
~160 ms glass-to-glass latency per a Feb 2026 audio-AI survey - faster than average human turn-taking, and it avoids the cascade's loss of tone and hesitation.
Models interruptions as two separate audio streams instead of an epoch-flush on a playback ring.
Trade-off vs Skadoosh: 7B model, GPU-class hardware, no tool/RAG/plugin framework around it.
The Python equivalent of Skadoosh's VAD+STT half: VAD, wake word, instant transcription; 10,158 stars, MIT. Its RealtimeTTS sibling is 4,040 stars, MIT.

Its own 2026 CPU guidance names sherpa-onnx Nemotron-3.5 streaming (560 ms) + Parakeet TDT int8 as the production CPU profile - the Python ecosystem has moved to streaming ASR while Skadoosh still runs whole-utterance whisper.cpp behind a 300 ms silence gate.
Assembles from pip packages rather than one binary; latency tuning is the developer's job.
Reference Python implementation of the same TTS model Skadoosh uses (2,749 stars, MIT) - a useful cross-check for audio quality and voice keys.
Skadoosh phonemises through misaki-rs, a Rust port of the same misaki G2P, so output should be comparable with identical ONNX weights.
3,797 stars, MIT, last pushed 2024-11-15 - the cautionary tale: a well-starred voice-agent framework that effectively stopped shipping.
Good contrast for the 'is this project maintained?' section next to Skadoosh's own 404.
11,144 stars; targets latency-critical workloads with audio processing in C++, and ships TEN VAD for low-latency real-time agents.
Shares Skadoosh's native-core bet but keeps a Python surface and a live repository.
Direct Rust competitor: 'a cross-platform pipeline framework for building fully local, interruptible voice agents'.
Smaller and younger than Skadoosh but with a live homepage - worth a head-to-head in the same article.
Fully local voice agent in pure Rust that 'never leaves your machine' - identical positioning to Skadoosh, evidence that a local-first Rust voice-agent niche exists.
Useful as the 'what else is in this niche' reference rather than a feature comparison.

stats.fact: Skadoosh 0.12.1 was published 2026-08-23; the crate first appeared 2026-08-19 and shipped ~22 releases (0.1.0 → 0.12.1) in under a week.
Crate downloads total 389 (all-time as reported), with per-version counts in the 14–23 range — very early-stage adoption.
Zero reverse dependencies on crates.io as of 2026-10-01.
100% rustdoc coverage: 409/409 items documented, but only 4/210 items have examples. Package size 960.3 kB source; docs.rs build ~2m19s.

Declared repository https://github.com/Hot-Coco/Skadoosh returns HTTP 404 (checked unauthenticated AND with an authenticated gh token); the GitHub account/org 'Hot-Coco' also does not exist. docs.rs lists the owner as 'Hot-Coco' while crates.io lists the owner as TheLimeDev (Monster).

Default LLM is StealthyLM-Emotive (Qwen2.5-1.5B, 4-bit GGUF, 1.54B params), a small model fine-tuned by the same author; the README links huggingface.co/StealthyML/StealthyLM-Emotive, which redirects to Monster-Code/StealthyLM-Emotive (278 downloads, 1 like).
Skadoosh is dual-licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 and uses #![forbid(unsafe_code)] with rustls everywhere (no OpenSSL).

Key native dependencies: whisper-rs 0.15.1, ort 2.0.0-rc.13 (ONNX Runtime, Kokoro-82M TTS + all-MiniLM-L6-v2 RAG embedder), cpal 0.18, misaki-rs 0.3, aec-rs (echo cancellation), wasmtime 30 (WASM plugins).
Requires Rust 1.88+; binary install needs cmake, clang, libclang-dev, libasound2-dev, pkg-config and espeak-ng (for Kokoro TTS).

Peer Rust voice-agent projects by GitHub stars: EchoKit ~592, Sayna ~313, Vox ~46, pipecrab ~19, cydanix/voice-agent ~5, agentflow ~1. Skadoosh's own repo is unreachable (404) so no star count is verifiable.
Human conversational turn-taking averages ~200 ms across 10 languages (Stivers et al., PNAS 2009), which is why sub-800 ms is treated as acceptable and sub-400 ms as approaching human timing.
Cloud cascaded voice pipelines (hosted STT+LLM+TTS) typically total ~600 ms–1.7 s TTFA, and vendor benchmarks put real-world cloud voice agents between 420 ms (Synthflow) and 1,040 ms (Twilio Voice).

Kokoro-82M (the TTS Skadoosh uses) scores ELO 1059 on the Artificial Analysis Speech leaderboard — fractionally ahead of Cartesia Sonic 3 (1054) — and runs at ~80–120 ms TTFA on a MacBook M3 Pro with zero network/cost.
The conversational-AI market was $11.58B in 2024 and is projected to reach $41.39B by 2030 (23.7% CAGR); the voice-AI-agents segment grows at 34.8% CAGR.
Fully-local voice agents run at $0/min inference cost once deployed, versus roughly $0.10–$2.00 per minute for a cloud voice agent (STT+LLM+TTS+telephony).
skadoosh on crates.io: 389 all-time downloads; latest 0.12.1 published 2026-08-23; 23 versions released between 2026-08-19 and 2026-08-23.
Zero reverse dependencies on crates.io - nothing else in the Rust ecosystem depends on skadoosh.
The 0.12.1 crate tarball is 263,897 bytes / 93 files containing 22,255 lines of Rust across 83 .rs files, 188 #[test] functions and a Cargo.lock pinning 370 packages.

crates.io owner is TheLimeDev (GitHub account created 2025-04-16, 3 public repos, 11 followers, company field '@TeamAudiyo') while docs.rs attributes the crate to 'Hot-Coco' - two different identities on the same package.

Default LLM StealthyLM-Emotive now lives at huggingface.co/Monster-Code/StealthyLM-Emotive (278 downloads, 1 like, created 2026-08-21, last modified 2026-09-18); its card opens with 'Skadoosh unfortunately has been deprecated'.
Kokoro-82M, the default TTS, has 11,486,967 Hugging Face downloads and 7,074 likes, Apache-2.0, released 2024-12-26.
Silero VAD processes one 30+ ms audio chunk in under 1 ms on a single CPU thread, under an MIT license.
whisper.cpp, the engine under whisper-rs, needs 75 MiB disk / ~273 MB RAM for tiny and 466 MiB / ~852 MB for small.
Kokoro-82M CPU throughput: ONNX Runtime mean RTF 0.5711 (1.8x real time) versus PyTorch 0.7865 (1.3x) on 4 vCPU Intel Xeon / 15.6 GB, with UTMOS 4.44.

On two ARM cores (Neoverse-N1) Kokoro-82M runs at 0.87-0.93x real time - slower than it speaks; sentence splitting costs it ~8% throughput (0.51 s fixed cost per call) while Piper holds 8.2x on the same machine.
On GPU, Kokoro-82M reaches RTF ~0.03 (a 10-second clip in ~0.3 s), the lowest first-audio latency of the models benchmarked at that tier.

Qwen2.5-1.5B (the base of StealthyLM) on a CPU-only laptop via Ollama: 4-8 tokens/s, time-to-first-token 200-350 ms, and the LLM TTFT dominates the budget (VAD 0-5 ms, STT 50-150 ms, TTS TTFB 40-75 ms).
2026 voice-agent latency budget: STT 100-300 ms, LLM TTFT 350-1000 ms, TTS 90-200 ms, network 50-200 ms; under 500 ms feels natural, under 800 ms is acceptable, over 1000 ms reads as broken.

Practical 2026 targets: VAD/endpointing <30 ms, streaming ASR first partial <200 ms, LLM TTFT 300-400 ms, TTS first byte 150-200 ms, barge-in stop <200 ms, end-to-end TTFA <800 ms P95; LiveKit reports ~500-650 ms P95 for well-built pipelines.
A voice-agent phone call costs $0.30-$0.50 and cuts contact-center cost 60-70% on routine workflows; managed framework hosting is ~$0.01/min while models are ~$0.04/min (July 2026).
ElevenLabs raised a $500M Series D at an $11B valuation with ARR over $330M (Feb 2026) - the proprietary TTS benchmark the open-source stack is measured against.
Moshi runs at ~160 ms glass-to-glass latency with a 1.1 kbps Mimi codec - roughly 40 ms faster than average human conversational response.
Skadoosh's runtime dependency stack is mainstream and healthy: whisper-rs 1.37M downloads, cpal 22.3M, ort 20.2M, wasmtime 38.0M, misaki-rs 72K.
There is no Hacker News discussion of this Skadoosh: HN Algolia returns 0 hits for 'skadoosh voice' and for '"local voice agent" rust'.
Cascaded cloud voice pipelines typically total ~600 ms-1.7 s TTFA, with real-world cloud agents ranging from 420 ms (Synthflow) to 1,040 ms (Twilio Voice).
